---
title: "Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens"
subtitle: "Passes that pretend to be something else: the run fake, the quarterback on the move, and the throw that invites the rush in"
description: "The passing game's deception family: why play-action works (linebackers' run-fit triggers, glossed here and built in 05-05) and why the data says it does not need a successful run game; under-center versus shotgun play-action; the bootleg, the naked bootleg, the keeper, the leak and the shot play; the slow (running back) screen, tunnel, jailbreak, tight end and middle screens; how a screen differs from a swing or flare route; screen timing, the linemen's release and why screens punish pressure; and team play-action rates and efficiency from FTN charting data."
glossary:
  "Play-action": "A pass play that begins with a fake run, usually a fake handoff to a running back, so that linebackers and safeties step toward the line before they realize it is a pass."
  "Bootleg": "A play-action pass in which the quarterback fakes a run one way, then rolls out the other way with the ball, away from where the run fake sent the defense, toward receivers set at short, medium and deep levels on that side."
  "Naked bootleg": "A bootleg with no blocker assigned to protect the quarterback on the side he rolls to: it depends on the unblocked end chasing the run fake."
  "Keeper": "A quarterback run off a run fake: he shows the handoff, keeps the ball and runs, usually around the end the fake drew inside. On a bootleg it is the quarterback's choice to run when nobody has stayed outside to stop him; some playbooks also call the whole bootleg a 'keep'."
  "Leak": "A late release by a tight end or back who first sells a block or a run fake, then slips into the space the defense has abandoned, often running against the flow of the play (for example, back across the field behind a bootleg)."
  "Shot play": "A play built to throw deep, usually 20 or more yards downfield, called in a situation the offense has chosen for it; most are play-action passes with extra blockers and only two or three receivers in the pattern."
  "Screen": "A pass thrown to a receiver at or behind the line of scrimmage with blockers already set up in front of him. The defense is invited to rush or flow one way; then the blockers release to the other."
  "Slow screen": {def: "The classic screen to a running back: the linemen pass-block for a count or two and let the rushers through, the back pretends to block and slips out behind them, and the quarterback drifts back and throws over the rush to the back, with three linemen in front of him.", aliases: ["RB screen"]}
  "Tunnel screen": "A wide receiver screen in which the receiver comes back inside, toward the ball, and catches it behind the line between blockers: linemen who have released outward and a teammate blocking the defender outside him, which forms the 'tunnel' he runs through."
  "Jailbreak screen": "A screen in which some or all of the offensive linemen skip pass protection and sprint out to block in space at the snap, leaving the rushers free, while a receiver steps back to catch a quick throw behind them. Names vary by playbook; some teams call the tunnel screen a jailbreak."
  "Swing route": "A running back's route that bows backward, then out toward the sideline, so he catches the ball on the move behind or at the line of scrimmage. Unlike a screen, nobody is set up to block for him."
  "Flare": "A running back's quick release toward the sideline on a shallow arc that bends slightly upfield, used as a quarterback's outlet or to pull a linebacker wide. Many playbooks treat flare and swing as the same route."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import os
import logging
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Patch, RegularPolygon
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, routes as r, style

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
GREEN = "#0f7a55"           # a darker step of the aqua highlight, for text and read lines on the field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]    # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
GREY = style.MUTED
LINE_D, OFF_BALL, GUN, UC = -0.7, -1.5, -5.0, -1.9
OL = (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- players and alignments
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen, 1.6 yards apart, each lettered so the reader can follow him."""
    return [O(k, k, LINE_D, w, k) for k, w in OL]


def ace_tight():
    """12 personnel under center: tight ends U (left) and Y (right) on the line, receivers X and Z
    a step off the ball in tight splits, the back seven yards deep. Seven on the line: five
    linemen plus the two tight ends, who are the ends and so eligible."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                      O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                      O("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 9.0)]


def i_form():
    """21 personnel I formation: X on the line wide left, Y in-line right, Z off the ball wide right."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                      O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.0)]


def spread(rb_w=-1.5, y_inline=False):
    """11 personnel, shotgun 2x2: X and Z on the line wide, H in the left slot and Y (a tight end)
    in the right slot, both a step off the ball. y_inline=True attaches Y to the line instead and
    moves Z off the ball, so there are still exactly seven on the line."""
    out = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, rb_w, "R"),
                     O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.0)]
    if y_inline:
        return out + [O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.0)]
    return out + [O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15.0)]


def even_front(cb_w=10.0, shell="two"):
    """A four-man even front (named in 05-02) with linemen labelled by technique number, three
    linebackers and either two deep safeties (shell='two') or one, with the strong safety
    walked down into the box (shell='one': eight in the box)."""
    out = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, 0.7, "1"),
           D("BT", "DT", 1.0, -2.35, "3"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "5"),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -cb_w - 0.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, cb_w + 0.5, "CB")]
    if shell == "two":
        out += [D("FS", "FS", 11.5, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.5, 8.0, "SS")]
    else:
        out += [D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 6.5, 8.5, "SS")]
    return out


def nickel(extra=None, shell="three"):
    """A 4-2-5 nickel against the 2x2: corners off the outside receivers, the strong safety over H
    (left slot), the nickel ($) over Y (right slot), one deep safety. shell='zero' pulls the free
    safety down to eight yards over the back (no deep help) for all-out pressure looks.
    extra = {key: (d, w)} moves anyone."""
    out = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"),
           D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"),
           D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB"),
           D("SS", "SS", 5.5, -8.6, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 8.6, "$"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS") if shell == "three" else D("FS", "FS", 8.0, -2.0, "FS")]
    extra = extra or {}
    return [q.moved(d=extra[q.key][0], w=extra[q.key][1]) if q.key in extra else q for q in out]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- moving people
def go_to(p, key, end, kind="path", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a path, run, route, block, pull or rush."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "rush":
        return p.rush(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, pts, frame="field", delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def pass_set(p, keys=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"), depth=1.2, speed=None):
    """Linemen step back into their pass sets."""
    for k in keys:
        p.block(k, pts=[(-depth, 0.0)], speed=speed)


def zone_steps(p, keys=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"), step=(0.15, 1.3)):
    """Linemen take outside-zone steps to the right but stay at the line (the one-yard limit)."""
    for k in keys:
        p.block(k, pts=[step])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drawing helpers
def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def clean(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard numbers (they sit where players stand); clip all text to the window."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=6.2, ax=None, **kw):
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, title=False, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.2, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13,
                fontweight=weight, linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9) if box else None)


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13, linespacing=1.15,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def branch(fld, p, pts, color=GREEN, lw=1.7, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed path through absolute (d, w) points: a defender's reaction, or the other branch of a read."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=5, solid_capstyle="round")
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=5))
    elif end == "tee":
        v = np.array([xs[-1] - xs[-2], ys[-1] - ys[-2]])
        perp = np.array([-v[1], v[0]]) / np.linalg.norm(v) * 0.75
        fld.ax.plot([xs[-1] - perp[0], xs[-1] + perp[0]], [ys[-1] - perp[1], ys[-1] + perp[1]],
                    color=color, lw=lw + 0.6, zorder=5)


def ring(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE, r_=1.25):
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), r_, fc="none", ec=color, lw=1.8, zorder=7))


def opening(fld, p, center, size, color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.2):
    """A soft green oval: the space that opens. size = (depth, width) in yards."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, *center)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), size[1], size[0], fc=color, alpha=alpha, ec=color, lw=1.0,
                             zorder=1.6))


def badge(fld, p, d, w, n, color=GREEN):
    """A small numbered circle: step n of a sequence."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), str(n), fontsize=7.5, color="white", fontweight="bold", ha="center",
                va="center", zorder=14, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.22", fc=color, ec="white", lw=0.6))


def panel_title(ax, text, fs=9):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=fs, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


LEGEND = {
    "route": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, label="route"),
    "block": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.8, marker="|", ms=8, mew=2.2, label="block"),
    "run": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.6, label="ball carrier"),
    "fake": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.6, label="fake / QB path"),
    "pass": Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), label="the throw"),
    "react": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2.2)), label="defender's reaction"),
    "rush": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8, label="rush / defender's path"),
    "other": Line2D([], [], color=GREEN, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (3, 2.2)), label="the other option"),
    "window": Patch(fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.25, ec=style.THIRD, label="space that opens"),
}


def legend(fig, keys, ncol=None, y=0.0, fs=7):
    hs = [LEGEND[k] for k in keys]
    fig.legend(handles=hs, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=ncol or len(hs), fontsize=fs,
               frameon=False, handlelength=2.0, columnspacing=1.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- frame strips (print) and video (web)
MARK_R = 0.7


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window_, rings=(), throw_t=None, mark_r=MARK_R):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, faint trails, optional rings and the ball's flight so far."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window_, numbers=False, hashes=True,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window_[0] + 0.4, play.los + window_[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.45, zorder=3)
    if throw_t is not None and t > throw_t:
        b = df[(df["side"] == "ball") & (df["frameId"] <= fid)]
        b = b[b["time"] >= throw_t - 0.05]
        xs, ys = fld.xy(b["x"].values, b["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, rr in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"]))
        if rr["side"] == "ball":     # drawn beside the carrier's marker so it never hides his label
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x + mark_r * 1.15, y + mark_r * 0.55), 0.95, 0.6, fc=style.BALL, ec="white",
                                 lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(rr.get("label", "") or "")
        if rr["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), mark_r, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=mark_r * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62) * mark_r / 0.7))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), mark_r * 1.7, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    return fld


def plan(fld, p, key, t0, color=None, lw=1.5, dashed=False):
    """The rest of a player's path from time t0 on (where he is going), ending in an arrowhead."""
    kf, _, _ = p._compile()
    t1 = float(kf[key][-1, 0])
    if t1 <= t0 + 0.05:
        return
    pts = np.array([p.position(key, tt) for tt in np.linspace(t0, t1, 50)])
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
    side = p.players[key].side
    col = color or (style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE)
    ls = (0, (3, 2)) if dashed else "-"
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-3], ys[:-3], color=col, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=4, solid_capstyle="round")
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-4], ys[-4]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                                     color=col, lw=lw, zorder=4))


def moment(ax, p, t, lateral, window, rings=(), plans=(), mark_r=0.8):
    """The play frozen at time t (faint trails show where everyone came from); `plans` adds
    each listed player's remaining path."""
    fld = frame_panel(ax, p, tracking(p), t, lateral, window, rings, mark_r=mark_r)
    for key in plans:
        plan(fld, p, key, t)
    return fld


def throw_arrow(fld, p, a, b):
    """The throw, drawn by hand from (d, w) a to (d, w) b."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, *a), _P(fld, p, *b)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=9, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=9,
                                     connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.08"))


def throw_at(p, key, t_catch):
    """Schedule the pass so the ball reaches `key` at about t_catch (ball speed 18 yd/s)."""
    t = t_catch - 0.6
    for _ in range(5):
        a, b = p.position("QB", t), p.position(key, t_catch)
        t = t_catch - float(np.hypot(*(b - a))) / 18.0
    p.pass_to(key, t=round(t, 2))
    return round(t, 2)


def strip(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-24, 4), window=(-8, 14), ncols=2, rings=(), throw_t=None,
          width_in=6.5):
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]), window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.62 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, throw_t)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.3,
                    color=style.INK, linespacing=1.2)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.4 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-24, 4), window=(-8, 14), rings=(), throw_t=None, width_in=5.6):
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]), window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, throw_t)
        txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        if notes:
            cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def play_movie(play, times, notes=None, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        kw.pop("ncols", None)
        kw.pop("width_in", None)
        video(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (dropbacks with FTN play-action and screen charting, 2022-2025)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
PCOLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "qb_dropback", "qb_spike", "pass_attempt",
         "sack", "qb_scramble", "epa", "success", "air_yards", "yards_after_catch", "complete_pass",
         "receiver_player_id", "play_type", "qb_kneel", "down", "rusher_player_id"]
FCOLS = ["game_id", "play_id", "is_play_action", "is_screen_pass", "qb_location", "is_qb_out_of_pocket",
         "n_pass_rushers"]

plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PCOLS)
plays = plays[(plays["season_type"] == "REG") & plays["down"].notna() & plays["epa"].notna()]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(SEASONS).to_pandas().rename(
    columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})
DB = plays[(plays["qb_dropback"] == 1) & (plays["qb_spike"] != 1)].merge(ftn[FCOLS], on=["game_id", "play_id"],
                                                                        how="inner")
DB["pa"] = DB["is_play_action"].astype(bool)
DB["screen"] = DB["is_screen_pass"].astype(bool)
DB["oop"] = DB["is_qb_out_of_pocket"].astype(bool)

# league play-action numbers
by_season = DB.groupby(["season", "pa"])["epa"].mean().unstack()
PA_RATE = DB.groupby("season")["pa"].mean()
D25 = DB[DB["season"] == 2025]
PA_EPA25, NO_EPA25 = D25.loc[D25["pa"], "epa"].mean(), D25.loc[~D25["pa"], "epa"].mean()
PA_SR25, NO_SR25 = D25.loc[D25["pa"], "success"].mean(), D25.loc[~D25["pa"], "success"].mean()
UC_PA25 = D25.loc[D25["qb_location"] == "U", "pa"].mean()
GUN_PA25 = D25.loc[D25["qb_location"] == "S", "pa"].mean()
loc = DB[DB["qb_location"].isin(["U", "S"])].groupby(["qb_location", "pa"])["epa"].mean().unstack()
loc_n = DB[DB["qb_location"].isin(["U", "S"])].groupby(["qb_location", "pa"]).size().unstack()
comp = DB[(DB["pass_attempt"] == 1) & (DB["sack"] == 0)]
YAC = comp.groupby("pa")["yards_after_catch"].mean()
AIR = comp.groupby("pa")["air_yards"].mean()
OOP = DB.groupby("pa")["oop"].mean()
SACK = DB.groupby("pa")["sack"].mean()

# team-level, 2025
team25 = D25.groupby("posteam").agg(rate=("pa", "mean"), n=("epa", "size"))
team25["epa_pa"] = D25[D25["pa"]].groupby("posteam")["epa"].mean()
team25["epa_no"] = D25[~D25["pa"]].groupby("posteam")["epa"].mean()
team25["gain"] = team25["epa_pa"] - team25["epa_no"]
team25["n_pa"] = D25[D25["pa"]].groupby("posteam").size()
N_BETTER25 = int((team25["gain"] > 0).sum())
TOP_RATE = team25["rate"].idxmax()
RANK = team25["rate"].rank(ascending=False, method="min")
ordinal = lambda n: f"{n}{'th' if 10 <= n % 100 <= 20 else {1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd'}.get(n % 10, 'th')}"  # noqa: E731
TOP_GAIN = team25["gain"].idxmax()

# does play-action need a run game? team-seasons, running back carries only
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(SEASONS).to_pandas()
pos_of = rosters.drop_duplicates("gsis_id").set_index("gsis_id")["position"]
backs = set(rosters.loc[rosters["position"].isin(["RB", "FB"]), "gsis_id"].dropna())
runs = plays[(plays["play_type"] == "run") & (plays["qb_kneel"] == 0) & (plays["qb_scramble"] == 0)
             & plays["rusher_player_id"].isin(backs)]
ts = runs.groupby(["season", "posteam"]).agg(rush_epa=("epa", "mean"))
ts["run_rate"] = plays[plays["play_type"].isin(["run", "pass"])].assign(
    r=lambda x: (x["qb_dropback"] == 0)).groupby(["season", "posteam"])["r"].mean()
g = DB.groupby(["season", "posteam", "pa"])["epa"].mean().unstack()
ts["gain"] = g[True] - g[False]
ts["rate"] = DB.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["pa"].mean()
ts = ts.dropna()
R_RUSH = ts["rush_epa"].corr(ts["gain"])
R_RATE = ts["run_rate"].corr(ts["gain"])
SHARE_POS = (ts["gain"] > 0).mean()

# screens, by number of pass rushers (FTN), pass attempts only
att = DB[DB["pass_attempt"] == 1].copy()
att["rpos"] = att["receiver_player_id"].map(pos_of)
att["rushers"] = att["n_pass_rushers"].clip(3, 6)
SCR = att.groupby(["screen", "rushers"]).agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean")).reset_index()
RBS = att[att["screen"] & (att["rpos"] == "RB")].groupby("rushers").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"))
SCREEN_SHARE = att.groupby("season")["screen"].mean()
SCR_RB_SHARE = (att.loc[att["screen"], "rpos"] == "RB").mean()
kc = att[att["screen"]].groupby("posteam").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean")).sort_values("n", ascending=False)
LG_SCREEN_EPA = att.loc[att["screen"], "epa"].mean()
pct = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.0f}%"   # noqa: E731
```

Second-and-3 near midfield, early in the third quarter. The offense has run the ball on six of
its last eight snaps, and every time the defense's linebackers have shot forward at the snap and met
the running back near the line. Now the quarterback takes the snap from under center, turns his back
to the defense and pushes the ball into the running back's belly. Both linebackers take two hard steps
toward the line, exactly as they have all afternoon. But the quarterback pulls the ball back out, spins
the other way and runs toward the sideline, alone. The tight end who seemed to be blocking on the right
side is now crossing the field ten yards downfield, behind the linebackers, waving his hand. The
throw is easy, the catch is easy, and he runs another fifteen yards before anyone touches him. On the
replay, the analyst circles a linebacker's feet: two steps forward, then a desperate turn. *That* is
what this chapter is about: the passes that work by pretending to be something else.

**You'll be able to…**

- Explain why a run fake moves linebackers even against a team that cannot run, and what the
  data says about the old rule that you must "establish the run" first.
- Tell under-center from shotgun play-action, and a bootleg from a naked bootleg, a keeper, a leak
  and a shot play, from the first two seconds of a broadcast.
- Draw the running back's slow screen, the tunnel and jailbreak screens, the tight end screen and
  the middle screen, and tell any screen from a swing or flare route.
- Explain how a screen is timed, how the linemen release, and why screens get *better* the more
  defenders rush.
- Read a team's play-action rate and efficiency from charting data, and say which offenses lean on
  deception most.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd):** how pass concepts stretch a defender high and
  low or side to side, the quarterback's progression, crossing routes, and the
  [yankee](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yankee) shot concept (a deep post paired with a deep
  crosser). Play-action passes are mostly those concepts with a fake in front.
- **[Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd):** [outside (wide) zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-outside-zone),
  the line stepping sideways together, the linebackers flowing with it, the unblocked backside end, and
  the first look at why outside zone and the bootleg are a matched pair.
- **[Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd):** the [pocket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket),
  the [launch point](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-launch-point) (where the quarterback sets his feet
  to throw), [max protect](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-max-protect), and
  [time to throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-time-to-throw).
- **[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd):**
  [EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) (how much a play changed the offense's expected points;
  above zero is good for the offense) and [success rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate),
  for the data sections.

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares; *left* and *right* are
the offense's. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the offensive linemen, Q the quarterback, R the running back
and F the fullback. **Y** and **U** are tight ends, **X** and **Z** wide receivers, and **H** a slot
receiver. On defense, linemen are labelled by technique number in the under-center pictures and as T
(tackle) and E (end) in the shotgun ones; S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, CB a
cornerback, $ the nickel back, and FS and SS the safeties. Thin arrows are routes and paths, the thick
dark arrow is the ball carrier, lines ending in a short bar are blocks, dashed orange lines are what a
defender does in reaction, and the dashed brown arrow is the throw. The animations are simulated
plays in Big Data Bowl coordinates (more on that at the end of the chapter).

## Why a fake works: the linebacker's dilemma

Start with the defender who is being fooled, because play-action is really a play *on him*.

A linebacker lines up about four or five yards off the ball, and on every snap he has two jobs that
pull in opposite directions. Against a run he has a **gap** to fill (a [run fit](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-run-fit),
the defense's plan for who fills which gap, built in [Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)),
and he has to get into it *fast*: a running back hits the line about a second after the snap, and a
linebacker who waits to be sure arrives after the back has gone by. Against a pass he has a zone or a man
to cover, which usually means running *backward*, to a spot ten yards deep or to a receiver.

He cannot wait to find out which job it is. So he is taught to decide from a **key**, one or two
players whose first step tells him run or pass ([key](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-key-read-key-defense)
reading is the subject of [Linebackers](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd)).
The usual keys are the offensive guard in front of him and the backfield. A guard who fires forward
with his pads low means run. A guard who pops up and steps backward into a pass set means pass. A
running back heading for the line with the quarterback's hands reaching toward him means run. Those
first-step signals are the linebacker's **run-fit triggers**: the moment he sees them, he attacks
his gap. Coaches call a linebacker who reacts fast to them a "downhill" player, and they love him,
because against the run he is right.

[**Play-action**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action), a pass play that begins with a fake run, is
built to pull those triggers on purpose. The guard fires out as if run-blocking. The
running back takes the same path he takes on the real run. The quarterback reaches the ball out to him
and pulls it back. For about a second, every signal the linebacker has been trained to trust says
*run*. By the time he sees the quarterback still holding the ball, he has taken two or three steps
forward, and he now has to stop, turn around and run back to a spot ten yards behind him. That
second is the play.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lb-void
#| fig-cap: "What one second of a fake buys. Both panels freeze the play 1.5 seconds after the snap; faint lines show the path each player has taken so far, and the blue arrow is the rest of Z's route, a dig (an in-breaking route at 13 yards). Left, a straight dropback: the linemen set back in pass protection, the linebackers read it at once and drop about ten yards deep, right in the dig's path. Right, play-action: the line steps forward as if run-blocking, the back takes the handoff path, and the linebackers step up toward the line before turning back (see their faint trails). They are only about five yards deep, and the space behind them, where the dig crosses, is empty (green)."
T_LOOK = 1.5
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.9))
for ax, pa in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=None)
    go_to(p, "Z", (13.0, -3.0), "route", via=[(12.6, 9.0)])
    if pa:
        zone_steps(p, keys=("U", "LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y"))
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.5), via=[(-2.4, -0.4)], speed=3.4)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-7.4, -1.2), speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.7, 4.3), via=[(-4.3, 2.4)], speed=5.5)
        for k, step, back in (("MIKE", (3.0, 3.2), (6.6, 1.2)), ("WILL", (3.1, -1.2), (6.6, -3.0)),
                              ("SAM", (2.9, 7.8), (6.4, 8.4))):
            go_to(p, k, step, speed=4.0)
            go_to(p, k, back, speed=3.0, delay=0.2)
    else:
        pass_set(p, speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-7.4, 0.0), speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-5.4, -1.6), speed=2.5)
        for k, end in (("MIKE", (10.4, 2.6)), ("WILL", (10.2, -4.4)), ("SAM", (9.2, 6.0))):
            go_to(p, k, end, speed=5.0)
    fld = moment(ax, p, T_LOOK, lateral=(-13.0, 13.0), window=(-9.5, 17.5), plans=("Z",), mark_r=0.75)
    if pa:
        opening(fld, p, (11.0, 2.0), (6.0, 14.0))
        say(fld, p, 15.6, 1.0, "empty: the LBs\nstepped up first", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -7.6, 7.0, "the run fake", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Play-action: LBs about 5 yd deep")
    else:
        say(fld, p, 15.6, 1.0, "LBs sit in\nthe dig's path", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -7.6, 7.0, "pass set: LBs see it", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Dropback: LBs about 10 yd deep")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Compare the two panels of @fig-lb-void. The receiver runs the same route in both. On the dropback,
three linebackers are sitting at about the depth of his break, and the quarterback has to fit the ball
between them. On the play-action pass, those same three linebackers are five yards shallower when the
ball needs to arrive, and they are moving the wrong way. The window is not a little bigger. It is a
different play.

### The fake has rules too

Two rules shape what the fake can look like, and both come from the offensive line.

First, **the linemen cannot go downfield.** On a pass that is thrown beyond the line of scrimmage, an
offensive lineman may not be more than one yard past the line when the ball is thrown; if he is, it is
a foul ([illegal man downfield](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-man-downfield), taught in
[Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd)).[^ineligible] So a play-action line cannot really run-block the
way it would on a run, driving defenders five yards back. It has to *look* like run blocking while
staying at the line: aggressive, low first steps, then holding its ground. Coaches call this a
"run-action" protection, and the best ones are nearly indistinguishable from the run for the first
step or two, which is all the linebacker reads.

Second, **the defensive line is not fooled for long.** A defensive lineman fights the blocker in front
of him on every snap, and he feels pass protection the instant the blocker stops moving forward. That
is why play-action does not buy the quarterback extra *protection*; it buys him *space behind the
linebackers*. In fact the quarterback is a little more exposed: he has turned his back or spent half a
second faking, and he still has to set up and throw.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Defenses have to stop the run quickly, so the defenders closest to the line are trained to react to the
first signs of a run. Play-action turns that training into a weakness: it shows them those signs on a
pass, gets them moving forward, and throws into the space they left. The price is time and protection.
The fake takes half a second, the quarterback's back is often to the defense, the linemen are limited
to the line, and the defensive linemen are not fooled at all. Play-action trades a little safety at the
quarterback's spot for a lot of open grass downfield.
:::

## "You have to establish the run." Do you?

Every broadcast you have ever watched has an announcer who says play-action works because the team has
been running the ball well: the linebackers have been *punished* by the run, so they bite on the fake.
It sounds like common sense. It is, mostly, not true.

The cleanest test came from Ben Baldwin, an analyst who later helped build the nflfastR play-by-play
models this course uses. In 2018 he looked at whether a team's play-action passes did better when its run
game had been working, measured several ways (rushing success that season, in that game, earlier on that
drive) and found essentially no relationship: play-action passes beat ordinary dropbacks by about the same
margin whether the run game was good, bad or barely used.[^baldwin] Josh Hermsmeyer, then writing for
FiveThirtyEight, added the mechanism: linebackers react to run *action* on almost every snap, because
reacting is their job, not because they have been convinced by a running back's stats.

You can rerun the test with the data this course uses. FTN's charters mark every dropback as play-action or
not, and nflverse joins it to the play-by-play. Over 2022–2025, play-action dropbacks averaged
`{python} f"{DB.loc[DB['pa'], 'epa'].mean():+.3f}"` EPA against `{python} f"{DB.loc[~DB['pa'], 'epa'].mean():+.3f}"`
for other dropbacks (essentially zero), and the gap was there in every one of the four seasons.[^ftn] @fig-pa-run-game asks Baldwin's question of
every team-season.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pa-run-game
#| fig-cap: "Does play-action need a good run game? Each dot is one team-season, 2022-2025 (128 in all). Across: how well the team's running backs ran the ball (EPA per carry). Up: how much better the team's play-action dropbacks were than its other dropbacks (EPA per dropback, play-action minus the rest). If a run game 'set up' play-action, the dots would climb to the right. They do not: the best and worst running teams got about the same boost from the fake. Data: nflverse play-by-play with FTN charting via nflreadpy; regular season."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.9))
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(ts["rush_epa"], ts["gain"], s=22, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.55, edgecolor=style.SURFACE,
           lw=0.5, zorder=3)
b, a = np.polyfit(ts["rush_epa"], ts["gain"], 1)
xx = np.linspace(ts["rush_epa"].min(), ts["rush_epa"].max(), 2)
ax.plot(xx, a + b * xx, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.8, zorder=4)
ax.annotate(f"best-fit line (r = {R_RUSH:+.2f}): a slight tilt\nthat explains about {100 * R_RUSH ** 2:.0f}% of the spread",
            (xx[1], a + b * xx[1]), xytext=(-4, 30), textcoords="offset points", ha="right", fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK_2, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
ax.axhline(ts["gain"].mean(), color=style.SERIES[0], lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.text(xx[1], ts["gain"].mean() - 0.014, f"average boost {ts['gain'].mean():+.2f}",
        fontsize=7.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="top", ha="right",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
ax.set_xlabel("Running back EPA per carry (team-season)", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_ylabel("Play-action boost\n(EPA per dropback)", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("A team's run game does not predict its play-action boost", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The correlation between a team's rushing efficiency and its play-action boost was
`{python} f"{R_RUSH:+.2f}"`, which is as close to nothing as real data gets, and play-action beat the
team's other dropbacks in `{python} pct(SHARE_POS)` of team-seasons. Teams that *ran more often* did see a
slightly bigger boost (correlation `{python} f"{R_RATE:+.2f}"`), which makes sense: a team that runs a
lot shows the defense the run *look* a lot, and its fakes match its runs. But being *good* at running was
not what mattered.

So what does matter? Coaches who build play-action games answer in one sentence: **the fake has to look
exactly like your real run**. Same formation, same line steps, same back's path, same quarterback
footwork. A linebacker is not reading the season's rushing stats. He is reading a guard's helmet and a
running back's first two steps, and if those match the run he has seen all day, he moves.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Play-action only works once the run game is working." The data says the fake's effect barely depends on
how well a team runs. What it depends on is how *similar* the fake is to the run, and to a lesser degree
how often the defense sees that run look. A team with a poor run game can still have an excellent
play-action game, and many have. The flip side: a fake that looks different from the real run (a sloppy
handoff motion, linemen who pop up into pass sets) gets little, however many yards the back has.
:::

## Under center or shotgun: two kinds of fake

The quarterback's starting spot changes what the fake can be, and you can see the difference from the
couch in the first half-second.

```{python}
#| label: fig-uc-vs-gun
#| fig-cap: "Two kinds of fake. Left, under center: the quarterback opens, turns his back to the defense and extends the ball to the back on the outside-zone path (1), then turns around, finds the defense and sets up seven or eight yards deep (2). For about a second he cannot see the field. Right, shotgun: the back runs across the quarterback's face, the quarterback rides the ball into his belly (1) and pulls it, never turning his head away from the defense (2). The fake is quicker, but it looks less like a real handoff, and the defense knows it."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, uc in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    off = [q for q in (ace_tight() if uc else spread(rb_w=-2.0)) if q.key in (*dict(OL), "QB", "RB")]
    dfn = [q for q in even_front() if q.key in ("PE", "PT", "BT", "BE", "MIKE", "WILL")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    zone_steps(p)
    if uc:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=3.0)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-7.4, -1.4), speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-1.8, 4.7), via=[(-4.4, 2.3)])
    else:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-5.4, 0.7), speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-7.0, 0.2), speed=3.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.2, 4.0), via=[(-4.3, 0.7)])
    p.read("RB", key="MIKE")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.5, 8.5), window=(-9.5, 6.5))
    if uc:
        badge(fld, p, -2.6, 3.0, 1)
        say(fld, p, -3.6, -5.6, "back to the\ndefense", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        badge(fld, p, -8.8, -2.8, 2)
        say(fld, p, -8.2, -5.0, "turn, find the\ndefense, set", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "Under center: a full fake")
    else:
        badge(fld, p, -3.6, 2.2, 1)
        badge(fld, p, -8.2, 1.4, 2)
        say(fld, p, -8.2, -4.8, "eyes downfield\nthe whole time", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "Shotgun: a ride and a pull")
    say(fld, p, 5.3, 5.0, "M reads\nthe back", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**Under center**, the quarterback takes the snap, turns and carries out the same footwork as a real
handoff, often with his back fully to the defense, and the running back's path is identical to the run.
It is the most convincing fake in football, because it *is* the run for the first second. The cost is that
the quarterback loses sight of the defense, then has to whip around, find his receivers and throw, often
with a defensive lineman closing. Plays from under center are therefore usually built with a simple
read the quarterback can find quickly after he turns.

**From the shotgun**, the back runs across the quarterback's face and the quarterback "rides" the ball
into his belly for a beat, the same mesh as a shotgun run. The quarterback never stops seeing the
defense, and the throw can come sooner. But a shotgun fake looks less like a run, partly because
defenses know that most shotgun plays are passes.

The numbers make the split vivid. In 2025, `{python} pct(UC_PA25)` of all dropbacks from under center
used play-action, against `{python} pct(GUN_PA25)` from the shotgun. Under center has become, in effect, the
play-action formation, which is a big reason it came back into fashion.[^ftn2] And play-action from under
center was the most productive kind of dropback in football. Over 2022–2025:

| Dropback from… | No fake | Play-action | Boost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under center | `{python} f"{loc.loc['U', False]:+.2f}"` | `{python} f"{loc.loc['U', True]:+.2f}"` | `{python} f"{loc.loc['U', True] - loc.loc['U', False]:+.2f}"` |
| Shotgun | `{python} f"{loc.loc['S', False]:+.2f}"` | `{python} f"{loc.loc['S', True]:+.2f}"` | `{python} f"{loc.loc['S', True] - loc.loc['S', False]:+.2f}"` |

: EPA per dropback by the quarterback's alignment and whether he faked a handoff, 2022–2025 regular seasons (FTN charting via nflverse). Under-center dropbacks without a fake are a small, unusual group (`{python} f"{int(loc_n.loc['U', False]):,}"` plays against `{python} f"{int(loc_n.loc['U', True]):,}"` with a fake). {#tbl-pa-location}

Read @tbl-pa-location with care: it is a description, not an experiment. Per play, the under-center fake was
worth the most (`{python} f"{loc.loc['U', True]:+.2f}"`). But compare each fake with dropbacks from the *same*
alignment and the shotgun fake added `{python} "at least as much" if (loc.loc['S', True] - loc.loc['S', False]) >= (loc.loc['U', True] - loc.loc['U', False]) else "less"`
(`{python} f"{loc.loc['S', True] - loc.loc['S', False]:+.2f}"` against `{python} f"{loc.loc['U', True] - loc.loc['U', False]:+.2f}"`).
That second comparison is shaky, because under-center dropbacks *without* a fake are a small, odd group (quick
throws against defenses expecting a run, for instance), which flatters their average. And offenses choose when
to fake: they tend to do it in good situations (early downs, defenses expecting run), so part of every boost
belongs to the situation rather than the fake. What the table does show is that the full fake from under
center, the one that looks most like a run, is the most productive dropback an offense has.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, play-action is a menu category: pick a play with "PA" in the name and the game handles the
fake. In real football the fake is a skill that the quarterback, the back and the linemen rehearse every
week, and it degrades if any one of them gets lazy. Quarterbacks are graded on their fakes. Running backs
are coached to carry out the fake for several steps after the quarterback has pulled the ball, often
running into the line with an empty hand, because a linebacker who sees the back stop knows instantly.
:::

## Where the fake sends the ball: three windows

What does the quarterback do with the second the fake bought? Look at where play-action completions end
up. Over 2022–2025, play-action passes traveled about as far in the air as other passes
(`{python} f"{AIR[True]:.1f}"` yards on average, against `{python} f"{AIR[False]:.1f}"`), but receivers
gained **`{python} f"{YAC[True]:.1f}"` yards after the catch** on them, against
`{python} f"{YAC[False]:.1f}"` on other passes.[^ftn3] The fake's main gift is not depth. It is catching the
ball with nobody in front of you, because the people who would have been in front of you stepped up.

That points to the three places a play-action pass usually goes:

1. **Behind the linebackers, in the middle.** The window in @fig-lb-void: crossing routes, digs and
   [shallow crosses](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shallow-cross) that cross the field 5–15 yards deep
   through the space the linebackers just vacated.
2. **Behind the safeties.** If a safety reads run and comes down to help, the deep post or the corner route
   behind him is open. This is the *shot play*, below.
3. **To the side the defense left.** Move the quarterback the other way with the ball, and the whole
   defense's flow is pointing at the wrong sideline. This is the bootleg.

## The bootleg: move the launch point away from the flow

You met the bootleg in [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) as outside zone's
partner, and its ancestor, the Wing-T's [waggle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-waggle), in
[Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd). Here is
the full play.

A [**bootleg**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bootleg) is a play-action pass in which the quarterback
fakes a run one way and then rolls out the *other* way with the ball, toward a group of receivers set up at
three depths on that side. The name is usually explained by the quarterback hiding the ball on his hip as
he rolls away, the way a Prohibition bootlegger hid a bottle.[^bootname] Two things make it work at once:

- **The run fake** pulls the linebackers and safeties toward the run side.
- **The rollout** moves the quarterback's [launch point](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-launch-point)
  away from that side, so the pass rush, which is aimed at where he *was*, has to turn around and chase.

The classic route combination is a *flood* of the boot side at three depths (the
[flood](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood) idea of [Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)):
a short route to the **flat** (the area near the sideline just past the line), a **crosser** coming all the
way across the field from the other side at 8–12 yards, and a deep route, often a deep crosser called the
**over** route, 15 or more yards down. A receiver on the boot side runs deep straight away to clear out the
cornerback. That gives the quarterback a simple read on the move: deep if it is there, crosser if the
linebackers are trailing, flat if anyone comes at him.

Watch it move.

```{python}
#| label: fig-boot-animation
#| fig-cap: "The outside-zone bootleg, frame by frame (simulated, BDB-format; faint lines show each player's path so far). The offense shows the same two-tight-end look and the same first steps as outside zone right (03-02). (1) The line steps right, the back takes the fake, and the Mike and Will (ringed) step up and flow with it. (2) The quarterback has pulled the ball and is rolling left; the backside end chased the fake and is now behind him. (3) The Y, who started on the right side as a blocker, crosses the field behind the linebackers, who are turning to chase; the U is in the flat and Z on a deep over route. (4) The ball goes to the Y on the move, with room to run."
def boot_play():
    p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    zone_steps(p)
    # the fake: reverse out, ball to the back on the outside-zone path, then boot left
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=3.4)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, -8.0), speed=4.8, via=[(-5.0, -3.0)], delay=0.05)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.4, -11.5), speed=3.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.0, 6.8), via=[(-4.3, 2.4), (-1.9, 4.9)], speed=6.0)
    # the routes: flat (U), crosser (Y), deep over (Z), clear-out (X)
    go_to(p, "U", (3.0, -15.0), "route", via=[(-0.2, -5.6), (0.8, -8.5)], delay=0.5)
    go_to(p, "Y", (11.5, -22.0), "route", via=[(0.2, 5.6), (1.6, 3.6), (5.6, -0.8), (10.2, -8.0), (11.2, -15.0)],
          delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "Z", (19.0, -13.0), "route", via=[(10.0, 8.0), (15.5, 1.0)])
    go_to(p, "X", (22.0, -10.0), "route")
    # the defense believes the run
    go_to(p, "PE", (1.2, 6.2), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "PT", (1.1, 2.0), speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "BT", (0.9, -0.9), speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "BE", (-2.4, 1.0), via=[(0.4, -3.5), (-1.5, -2.6)], speed=4.2)         # chases the fake ...
    go_to(p, "BE", (-5.6, -7.0), speed=4.6, delay=0.1)                              # ... then turns, too late
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 3.6), speed=4.0)                                          # step up, flow ...
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.6, -4.0), speed=4.2, delay=0.35)                            # ... then turn and chase
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (5.8, -8.5), speed=4.6, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (2.8, 8.2), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (4.6, 3.5), speed=3.5, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "SS", (7.5, 6.5), speed=4.5)
    go_to(p, "SS", (10.0, -1.0), speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "FS", (10.0, -7.5), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "FS", (16.5, -5.0), speed=5.5)
    go_to(p, "LCB", (19.0, -10.5), speed=6.3, via=[(8.0, -10.5)])
    go_to(p, "RCB", (12.0, 4.0), speed=4.5)
    throw_at(p, "Y", 3.2)
    return p


bp = boot_play()
T_THROW = [e[2] for e in bp.ball_events if e[0] == "pass"][0]
play_movie(bp, [0.7, 1.7, 2.3, 3.2],
           notes=["the fake: line steps right,\nLBs step up and flow right",
                  "QB pulls it and boots left;\nthe end chased the fake",
                  "Y crosses behind the LBs;\nU in the flat, Z deep",
                  "ball to the Y on the move,\nroom to run"],
           rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE), ("Y", style.THIRD)),
           lateral=(-19.5, 12.5), window=(-9.5, 21.0), throw_t=T_THROW)
```

Look at frame 2 of @fig-boot-animation. Every defender's momentum is going one way and the quarterback is
going the other. The two linebackers who stepped up are now ten yards from the crosser and running
*backward* to catch him; the cornerback on the boot side has turned and run with the clear-out; the
backside end, the one man whose job was to stay home, chased the fake and is behind the play.

Now count the quarterback's options. All three receivers are on his side of the field, at three depths,
and he is moving toward them, which shortens every throw. The read is usually **high to low**: the over
route if the deep defender has gone with the clear-out, the crosser if the linebackers are trailing him,
and the flat if a defender comes up to stop the quarterback. If nobody comes up at all, he can run.

**Why the defense struggles.** It is not that the defenders are fooled for long. It is that they are fooled
at the *start*, when the decisive steps happen, and then the play moves away from them. A defense that has
been flowing hard to stop outside zone has been flowing correctly, every time, for three quarters. The
bootleg makes the correct reaction to the run the wrong reaction to the play.

**What the bootleg gives up.** The quarterback is throwing on the run, to only half the field, with fewer
receivers than a dropback (three, usually, sometimes four). Moving the launch point also moves it away from
most of the protection: on most boots, nobody is blocking the man the quarterback is running toward.

### The naked bootleg: nobody blocks the end

That last point is the bootleg's central bet, and the **naked** version makes it explicitly. A
[**naked bootleg**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-naked-bootleg) assigns *no one* to block the
defender on the boot side, usually the backside end, the man zone blocking leaves unblocked anyway. The
whole line and the back go with the run fake. The play is betting that the end will chase the fake, as he
has been taught to do on the real outside zone run.

```{python}
#| label: fig-naked-boot
#| fig-cap: "The naked bootleg's bet, frozen 1.8 seconds after the snap (faint lines: where players have been; arrows: where the receivers are going). The quarterback has faked outside zone right and is rolling left, and nobody is assigned to the backside end (ringed). Left: the end chased the fake down the line, so he is behind the quarterback, who has the edge: he can throw to any of his three receivers (U in the flat, Y crossing, Z deep) or, if nobody comes up, keep it and run (green dashes: the keeper). Right: the end stayed home and is attacking the quarterback. Now there is no time to read high to low; the quarterback throws to the flat at once (or throws the ball away)."
def naked(bites):
    p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    zone_steps(p)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=3.4)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, -8.0), speed=4.8, via=[(-5.0, -3.0)], delay=0.05)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.0, 6.8), via=[(-4.3, 2.4), (-1.9, 4.9)], speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "U", (3.0, -15.0), "route", via=[(-0.2, -5.6), (0.8, -8.5)], delay=0.5)
    go_to(p, "Y", (10.6, -14.0), "route", via=[(0.2, 5.6), (1.6, 3.6), (5.6, -0.8), (10.2, -8.0)], delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "Z", (17.0, -6.0), "route", via=[(10.0, 8.0), (15.5, 1.0)])
    go_to(p, "X", (17.0, -10.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 3.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (2.8, 8.2), speed=3.0)
    if bites:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-2.4, 1.0), via=[(0.4, -3.5), (-1.5, -2.6)], speed=4.2)
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-4.4, -6.4), via=[(0.0, -5.0), (-2.6, -5.8)], speed=3.6)
    return p


T_NB = 1.8
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.7))
for ax, bites in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    p = naked(bites)
    fld = moment(ax, p, T_NB, lateral=(-18.5, 11.5), window=(-10.0, 17.5), rings=(("BE", style.DEFENSE),),
                 plans=("U", "Y", "Z", "X"), mark_r=0.75)
    q = p.position("QB", T_NB)
    if bites:
        plan(fld, p, "QB", T_NB, color=style.OFFENSE)
        branch(fld, p, [(-6.2, -8.0), (-4.2, -11.6), (0.5, -13.2), (4.5, -13.6)])
        say(fld, p, -2.2, -15.4, "keeper", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 5.4, "end chased\nthe fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -8.6, -2.4, "Q: the edge\nis his", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "The end bites: throw or run")
    else:
        u = p.position("U", T_NB + 0.6)
        throw_arrow(fld, p, tuple(q), tuple(u))
        say(fld, p, -7.6, -12.6, "end stayed\nhome", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -8.6, 1.4, "Q: throw the\nflat now", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "The end stays home: get rid of it")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

When the bet wins (left panel of @fig-naked-boot), the naked boot is one of the easiest plays in football:
the quarterback is alone on the edge with three receivers and a defense running the wrong way. When it
loses (right panel), the quarterback has turned his back on a free defender. That is why the flat route is
always there and always first if the end stays home: it is the boot's built-in [hot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route)
throw, and the quarterback learns to check the end before anything else. It is also why offenses run naked
boots *after* the end has been chasing outside zone all day, not before.

### Keepers, protected boots and leaks

Three variations answer the obvious questions a defense asks of the bootleg.

**What if nobody covers the quarterback?** Then he runs. A [**keeper**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-keeper)
is a quarterback run off a run fake: he shows the handoff, keeps the ball and goes around the end the fake
drew inside. On a bootleg it is built in (the green branch in @fig-naked-boot): if the end chased and the
flat defender has run with the flat route, the quarterback's best option is often the empty grass in front
of him. Some teams also call keepers as designed runs, and some playbooks simply call the whole bootleg a
"keep." Either way, a quarterback who will run makes the defense pay for chasing the receivers.

**What if the end stops chasing?** Then the offense blocks him. A **protected** bootleg sends a blocker,
usually a guard pulling from the line or a tight end or fullback, to meet the end on the boot side, exactly
as the Wing-T's waggle did. The price is a tell: a guard running the "wrong" way, away from the run fake, is
the first thing a linebacker who keys the guards will see.

**What if the whole defense starts flowing to the boot?** Then throw back the other way. A
[**leak**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leak) is a late release by a tight end or back who first sells a
block, then slips into the space the defense has abandoned. On a bootleg, the classic leak is the
play-side tight end, who blocks the end for a count as if the run were real, then releases into the
flat on *his* side, the side the quarterback just ran away from.

```{python}
#| label: fig-boot-family
#| fig-cap: "Two answers to two defensive adjustments, each frozen mid-play (faint lines: where players have been; arrows: where they are going). Left, a protected bootleg at 1.6 seconds: against an end who will not chase, the left guard pulls (purple ring) and kicks him out, so the quarterback has a blocker on the boot side; the cost is that the pulling guard tips off linebackers who read the guards. Right, a boot leak at 2.1 seconds: against a defense that has learned to flow to the boot, the quarterback still rolls left and the receivers still flood that side, dragging the coverage with them (the defenders' faint orange trails all lead left), but the Y (green ring) blocked the end for a count and is now releasing into the right flat, where nobody is left; the quarterback will throw back across the field (dashed brown)."
def boot_variant(kind):
    p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    zone_steps(p, keys=("LT", "C", "RG", "RT") if kind == "protect" else ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"))
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=3.4)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, -8.0), speed=4.8, via=[(-5.0, -3.0)], delay=0.05)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-2.0, 5.4), via=[(-4.3, 2.4)], speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "U", (3.0, -15.0), "route", via=[(-0.2, -5.6), (0.8, -8.5)], delay=0.5)
    go_to(p, "Z", (17.0, -8.0), "route", via=[(10.0, 8.0), (15.5, 1.0)])
    go_to(p, "X", (17.0, -10.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 3.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (2.8, 8.2), speed=3.0)
    if kind == "protect":
        go_to(p, "Y", (10.6, -14.0), "route", via=[(0.2, 5.6), (1.6, 3.6), (5.6, -0.8), (10.2, -8.0)], delay=0.2)
        go_to(p, "LG", (-0.6, -5.2), "pull", via=[(-1.8, -2.2), (-1.6, -4.0)], speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "BE", (0.3, -5.6), speed=2.0)
    else:   # the coverage has learned to flow to the boot; the Y blocks, then leaks the other way
        go_to(p, "Y", (0.5, 5.4), "block", speed=1.0)
        go_to(p, "Y", (7.0, 12.0), "route", via=[(0.6, 8.8)], delay=0.6, speed=6.5)
        go_to(p, "PE", (0.9, 5.2), speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "PE", (-4.0, -2.0), speed=5.0, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "BE", (-0.2, -5.4), speed=2.0)
        for k, step in (("MIKE", (5.0, -4.0)), ("WILL", (5.0, -9.0)), ("SAM", (5.2, 1.0))):
            go_to(p, k, step, speed=4.5, delay=0.2)
        go_to(p, "SS", (13.0, -1.0), speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "RCB", (14.0, 3.0), speed=5.5)
        go_to(p, "FS", (14.0, -10.0), speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "LCB", (12.0, -14.5), speed=4.5)
        throw_at(p, "Y", 3.3)
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.8))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("protect", "leak")):
    p = boot_variant(kind)
    if kind == "protect":
        t = 1.6
        fld = moment(ax, p, t, lateral=(-18.5, 15.0), window=(-10.0, 18.0), rings=(("LG", PURPLE),),
                     plans=("U", "Y", "Z", "X", "QB"), mark_r=0.75)
        say(fld, p, -7.8, -12.6, "LG pulls and\nkicks out the end", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -7.6, 6.6, "a guard pulling away\nfrom the fake: a tell", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Protected boot")
    else:
        t = 2.1
        fld = moment(ax, p, t, lateral=(-18.5, 15.0), window=(-10.0, 18.0), rings=(("Y", style.THIRD),),
                     plans=("U", "Z", "X", "QB", "Y"), mark_r=0.75)
        te = [e[2] for e in p.ball_events if e[0] == "pass"][0]
        throw_arrow(fld, p, tuple(p.position("QB", te)), tuple(p.position("Y", 3.3)))
        say(fld, p, -3.0, 10.6, "Y: block,\nthen leak", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, 12.0, 11.0, "coverage flowed\nto the boot", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Boot leak: throw it back")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Each of these is a reply to a defensive reply, which is the pattern of this whole chapter (and of
[Constraint Theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)): the bootleg punishes
the end and linebackers for chasing the run; the protected boot and the keeper punish the defense for
adjusting to the boot; the leak punishes it for over-adjusting. None is a great play on its own. Together,
they make chasing, staying home and flowing all wrong some of the time, which is all an offense needs.

How much of this do offenses actually run? FTN charts whether the quarterback threw from outside the
pocket. From 2022 to 2025, the quarterback was out of the pocket on `{python} pct(OOP[True])` of play-action
dropbacks, against `{python} pct(OOP[False])` of the rest, and those include scrambles; the difference is
mostly designed boots and rollouts.

## The shot play: the fake that goes deep

The third window in the list above is behind the safeties. A [**shot play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shot-play)
is a play built to throw deep, usually 20 or more yards downfield, and called in a situation the offense
picked for it. Most shot plays share three features, and each has a reason.

- **Play-action**, because the deepest defender that matters is a safety, and a safety who reads run takes
  a step or two forward. A deep throw needs only that.
- **Extra blockers**, often [max protect](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-max-protect) with seven or eight
  men in protection, because a deep route takes three seconds or more to develop.
- **Only two or three receivers**, which is the price of the extra blockers. They are paired so that the one
  safety cannot cover both: in the classic [yankee](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yankee) concept, a deep
  post from one side and a deep over route from the other.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shot-play
#| fig-cap: "A play-action shot from the I formation against a single deep safety and eight defenders near the box. Eight blockers stay in: the five linemen, the Y, the fullback and, after his fake, the running back. Only two receivers go out: X on a deep post and Z on a deep over route (the yankee pairing). The fake pulls the linebackers and the strong safety forward and the free safety takes two steps up (dashed orange) before he can retreat. He cannot be in both places: if he stays on the post, the over is open in front of him (green dashes: the other throw); if he jumps the over, the post is behind him."
p = Play(i_form(), even_front(cb_w=13.5, shell="one"), los=35, to_go=None)
p.players["LCB"] = p.players["LCB"].moved(w=-14.5)
p.players["RCB"] = p.players["RCB"].moved(w=14.5)
zone_steps(p, step=(0.2, 0.3))
p.block("Y", pts=[(0.2, 0.2)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.0, 0.9), via=[(-2.4, -0.4)], speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-8.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.3, 1.6), via=[(-4.4, 0.9)])
go_to(p, "FB", (-2.6, -2.4), "block")
go_to(p, "X", (28.0, -1.0), "route", via=[(13.0, -14.0)])
go_to(p, "Z", (20.5, -12.0), "route", via=[(12.0, 14.0), (17.5, 6.0)])
p.pass_to("X", t=2.9)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-10.0, 31.5))
for k, end in (("MIKE", (2.4, 1.4)), ("WILL", (2.5, -2.4)), ("SAM", (2.3, 6.0)), ("SS", (3.6, 8.0))):
    q = p.players[k]
    branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6)
branch(fld, p, [(13.0, 0.0), (10.4, 0.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8)
branch(fld, p, [(-8.0, -0.9), (18.6, -8.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.5)
opening(fld, p, (24.5, -1.0), (6.0, 8.0))
opening(fld, p, (19.0, -8.5), (4.5, 7.5))
say(fld, p, 11.6, 6.2, "FS: two steps up", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 28.6, 4.8, "post", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 22.0, -12.6, "over", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -8.2, 7.4, "eight blockers,\ntwo receivers", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 5.0, -7.4, "LBs and SS\nattack the fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
fld.ax.legend(handles=[LEGEND["react"], LEGEND["pass"], LEGEND["other"], LEGEND["window"]], loc="upper center",
              bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=4, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

The defense in @fig-shot-play is the picture offenses want for a shot: one deep safety, the other safety
down near the box, and linebackers who attack the run. That defense is built to stop the run, and the
offense has usually spent the game showing it run looks from this exact formation. Situations matter as
much as looks. Coaches like shots on **second-and-short** (an incompletion leaves a manageable
third-and-short), right after a **turnover or a big play** (the defense is rattled and expects
conservatism), and when the defense has just moved a safety down to stop the run.

[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
showed that NFL offenses mostly *don't* take that second-and-short shot: they run, and when they pass,
they rarely throw deep. That is one reason the shot works when it comes. A defense that has seen
second-and-short handed off fifty times believes the fake.

**What the shot play gives up.** Two receivers against a defense with six or seven men in coverage is a
long-odds play on any single snap, and it has no answer if both routes are covered except a throwaway, a
scramble or a sack. Coaches accept a low completion rate for the size of the prize: one completion can be
worth more expected points than a whole series of short gains.

## Screens: let them come

Now the opposite trick. Play-action pretends to be a run so the defense steps *forward*. A
[**screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-screen) pretends to be a normal pass so the defense
rushes *in*, then throws the ball to a receiver at or behind the line with blockers already set up in
front of him. The rushers who came after the quarterback are now behind the play. The defenders left
in front are outnumbered by linemen.

The quick wide receiver screens, the [now screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-now-screen) and the
[bubble screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bubble-screen), were in [The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd):
the ball comes out at the snap and the blockers are other receivers. This section is about the screens that
use the **offensive linemen** as blockers, which changes everything about their timing.

A rule makes them possible. The one-yard limit on linemen downfield applies only to passes that are thrown
*beyond* the line of scrimmage. On a pass caught behind the line, the linemen can be ten yards downfield
when the ball is thrown, and on a screen they are.[^ineligible2]

### The slow screen

The original is the running back's screen, the [**slow screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slow-screen)
(also called the [**RB screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rb-screen)). It is "slow" because it is
built on patience: everyone on the offense pretends, for a count or two, that this is an ordinary dropback.

```{python}
#| label: fig-slow-screen
#| fig-cap: "The running back slow screen to the left, against a four-man rush (all eleven jobs). (1) The linemen set as if pass-blocking and give a soft punch, and the back pretends to block. (2) On a count of about one-and-a-half to two, the LT, LG and C let their rushers go and release left, two or three yards past the line; the back slides out behind them. (3) The quarterback drifts back to pull the rushers deeper, then lofts the ball over them. Blocking in front: the LT takes the first threat outside (here the Will), the LG the Mike, the C turns back for the first chaser, X runs his cornerback off, and H blocks the safety over him. The RG and RT keep blocking their men."
def slow_screen(p):
    """RB slow screen to the left: the line sets, the LT, LG and C release, the back slides out behind them."""
    for k in ("RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    # each sets and punches for a beat (the delay), then releases: the first man out takes the widest threat,
    # the next the man inside him, the center peels back for the first chaser
    go_to(p, "LT", (2.4, -8.4), "block", via=[(-1.7, -3.6)], speed=4.2, delay=0.45)
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.7, -4.6), "block", via=[(-1.7, -1.8)], speed=4.2, delay=0.45)
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.0, -4.6), "block", via=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=3.6, delay=0.45)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -2.6), speed=2.0)                                  # pretend to block ...
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.3, -7.0), "route", delay=0.45, speed=3.5, via=[(-4.6, -5.0)])  # ... then slide out
    go_to(p, "RB", (8.0, -6.3), "run", delay=0.12, via=[(1.0, -6.6)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-9.4, 0.4), speed=2.3)
    go_to(p, "X", (16.0, -15.5), "route")
    go_to(p, "H", (4.4, -11.4), "block", speed=3.0)
    kf, _, _ = p._compile()
    t_catch = float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][-1]) + 0.05
    throw_at(p, "RB", t_catch)
    return p


p = slow_screen(Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None))
for k, end in (("WDE", (-7.4, -2.6)), ("WDT", (-7.0, -0.2)), ("SDT", (-1.0, 2.0)), ("SDE", (-1.2, 4.4))):
    go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.6)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-19.5, 17.5), window=(-11.5, 17.5))
for k, end in (("WILL", (3.1, -8.2)), ("MIKE", (3.4, -4.8)), ("SS", (5.4, -11.6)), ("LCB", (13.0, -16.0))):
    q = p.players[k]
    branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
badge(fld, p, -2.6, 2.4, 1)
badge(fld, p, 0.9, -2.8, 2)
badge(fld, p, -10.2, 2.2, 3)
say(fld, p, -10.0, 7.4, "drift back: pull\nthe rush deeper", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -8.4, -10.8, "R: block a count,\nthen slide out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.0, 6.0, "rushers let through", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 10.6, -6.4, "three linemen\nout in front", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
fld.ax.legend(handles=[LEGEND["block"], LEGEND["run"], LEGEND["pass"], LEGEND["react"]], loc="upper center",
              bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=4, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

Walk through @fig-slow-screen in order, because the order is the play.

**Sell the dropback.** For the first second and a half, nothing looks unusual. The linemen pass-set,
the back steps up as if to pick up a blitzer, and the receivers run their routes, and those routes have a job:
pulling the cornerback and safeties deep and away from where the ball is going.

**Let them go.** Then the three linemen on the screen side deliberately lose. Each gives his rusher a
punch, then lets him run past toward the quarterback, and releases to the side. Line coaches teach the
release with a count (it varies by team, but roughly "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two"), because a
lineman who leaves too early tips the play off and one who leaves too late is still in the backfield when
the ball arrives. Each released lineman has a landmark and a rule: the first one out takes the widest
threat, the next one the next defender inside, the center the first defender chasing from behind.

**Pull the rush deep, then throw over it.** The quarterback keeps drifting back, eight, nine, ten yards,
dragging the rushers with him, then floats the ball over their heads to the back, who has slid out behind
the released linemen. The deeper the rushers chase, the farther they are from the catch.

**What the slow screen gives up.** It is a timing play with a lot of moving parts and a low margin for
error. If a rusher is *not* fooled (a defensive end who sees the tackle let go and stops to sit in the
throwing lane, which coaches call "smelling" the screen), the ball can be batted or intercepted near the
line. If the released linemen miss their landmarks, the back is running into a crowd. And it gives up the
whole downfield passing game for one snap: the quarterback has one place to throw.

### Swing and flare: not screens

Casual viewers call any short pass to a running back a screen. Most of them are not, and the difference
tells you what the offense was thinking.

```{python}
#| label: fig-swing-vs-screen
#| fig-cap: "Swing route or screen? Same formation, same defense, two different plays. Left, a swing route: the linemen stay in pass protection, nobody releases, and the back bows backward and out toward the sideline and catches the ball early, on the move, with the safety over the slot coming to meet him (dashed orange). He has to beat that man himself. Right, a slow screen: the back waits, the left side of the line releases in front of him, and when he catches it he has three blockers between him and the defense."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.4))
for ax, screen in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if screen:
        slow_screen(p)
    else:
        pass_set(p)
        p.dropback(1.6)
        p.route("RB", r.swing(9.0), side=-1)
        go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, -11.5), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(1.0, -11.0)])
        go_to(p, "H", (14.0, -9.0), "route")
        go_to(p, "X", (16.0, -15.5), "route")
        p._compile()
        t_c = float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][0])
        throw_at(p, "RB", t_c)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-19.5, 11.0), window=(-11.5, 17.5))
    if screen:
        say(fld, p, 10.6, -6.4, "three linemen\nin front", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -10.0, 4.6, "ball out\nat ~2.5 s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Slow screen: blockers out front")
    else:
        q = p.players["SS"]
        branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), (1.6, -11.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.5)
        say(fld, p, -3.4, 4.6, "the line keeps\npass-blocking", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -10.0, -11.0, "swing: ball out at\n~1 s, on the move", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 4.6, -15.6, "SS comes\nto meet him", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Swing route: no blockers")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

A [**swing route**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-swing-route) is a running back's route that bows
backward and then out toward the sideline, so he catches the ball on the move behind or at the line.
A [**flare**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flare) is a quicker, flatter release toward the sideline that
bends slightly upfield; many playbooks use the two words for the same thing. Either way, it is a pass
*route*: the line keeps blocking, nobody releases in front of the back, and the throw usually comes early.
