Its purposes are different from a screen's. It is an outlet when the downfield routes are covered (a
[checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown) the quarterback can always find), a way to pull a
linebacker wide and open the middle for another route, and a way to get a fast back the ball in space against
a slower linebacker.

The tell on a broadcast is the offensive line. **If any lineman is running downfield before the ball is
thrown, it is a screen** (or a run). If the line is still pass-blocking when the back catches it, it was a
route. The second tell is the timing: the swing is thrown in about a second, before the rush arrives; the
screen is thrown after the rush has arrived and gone by.

## The screen family

Once you see the slow screen's logic (let the rush come, release the linemen, throw behind them), the rest of
the family is variations on who catches it and where the blockers go.

### Tunnel and jailbreak: screens to a wide receiver

```{python}
#| label: fig-tunnel-jailbreak
#| fig-cap: "Two wide receiver screens that use the offensive line. Left, a tunnel screen to Z: Z takes two hard steps upfield to back his cornerback off, then comes back inside toward the ball and catches it behind the line. The Y blocks out on the cornerback; the RT and RG release outward and wall off the nickel and the Mike; Z runs up the 'tunnel' between them. Right, a jailbreak screen to H: at the snap the LT, LG and C skip pass protection entirely and sprint out to the left to form a wall in front of H, who steps back and catches a quick throw; the two rushers they would have blocked are left free (ringed). X blocks his cornerback."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("tunnel", "jail")):
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if kind == "tunnel":
        for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
        go_to(p, "RT", (2.0, 7.4), "block", via=[(-1.0, 4.4)], speed=4.0)      # wall off the nickel
        go_to(p, "RG", (2.8, 3.8), "block", via=[(-0.9, 2.6)], speed=4.0)      # wall off the Mike
        go_to(p, "Y", (4.4, 14.0), "block", speed=4.5)                          # block out on the corner
        go_to(p, "Z", (-1.0, 11.0), "route", via=[(2.0, 15.2)], speed=6.5)     # sell upfield, come back inside
        go_to(p, "Z", (11.0, 10.6), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(3.0, 10.4)])
        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "Z", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "Z" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        p.path("QB", [(-0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "SDE", (-3.6, 4.4), "rush", speed=3.4)
        go_to(p, "SDT", (-3.4, 1.4), "rush", speed=3.4)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.8, 20.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
        for k, end in (("NB", (3.0, 8.2)), ("MIKE", (3.6, 4.0)), ("RCB", (7.6, 15.0))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 9.0, 13.4, "the tunnel", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -5.6, 12.0, "Z: two steps up,\nthen back inside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Tunnel screen")
    else:
        go_to(p, "LT", (2.6, -12.0), "block", via=[(-0.4, -6.2)], speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, -8.4), "block", via=[(-0.4, -4.2)], speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "C", (3.8, -4.6), "block", via=[(-0.3, -1.6)], speed=5.0)
        for k in ("RG", "RT"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
        go_to(p, "H", (-0.2, -9.6), "route", speed=6.0)
        go_to(p, "H", (-2.0, -10.2), "route", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "H", (10.0, -10.6), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(2.0, -10.2)])
        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "H", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "H" and a.kind == "route"][-1]) + 0.05)
        go_to(p, "X", (3.0, -15.4), "block", speed=4.0)
        p.path("QB", [(-0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        for k, end in (("WDE", (-3.8, -2.2)), ("WDT", (-3.8, -0.4))):
            go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=4.5)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-20.5, 6.8), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
        for k in ("WDE", "WDT"):
            q = p.players[k]
            ring(fld, p, q.d, q.w, r_=1.2)
        for k, end in (("SS", (3.6, -12.4)), ("WILL", (4.0, -8.6)), ("MIKE", (4.4, -4.8))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, 8.8, -5.4, "linemen sprint\nout at the snap", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -7.0, -6.0, "rushers\nleft free", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "Jailbreak screen")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

A [**tunnel screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tunnel-screen) goes to an outside receiver who
comes back *inside*, toward the ball. The receiver's first steps upfield matter: the cornerback, seeing a
receiver attack him, backs up, and that cushion is the space the receiver catches the ball in. Two linemen
release outward to wall off the defenders inside, and a teammate (here the Y, a tight end in the slot, a
natural blocker) blocks the cornerback from the outside. The receiver catches it in the gap between them and
runs up the "tunnel."

A [**jailbreak screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jailbreak-screen) gets its name from what the line
does: at the snap, the linemen on the screen side do not pass-block at all, they break out and sprint toward
the screen side, leaving their rushers free. That makes it a *quick* screen, thrown in about a second, because
nobody is blocking those rushers. Its advantage over the now and bubble screens of 04-03 is size: instead of a
receiver trying to block a defender, a 310-pound lineman arrives in space against a 190-pound cornerback.
Playbook names in this family vary a lot. Some teams call the tunnel screen a jailbreak, and some call any
screen with the whole line releasing a "jailbreak." The ideas are what matter: who catches it, which way he
runs, and when the linemen leave.

### Tight end and middle screens

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-middle
#| fig-cap: "Two more members of the family (the receivers not involved are outside the picture). Left, a tight end screen: the Y blocks the end for a count, then slides out to the right flat behind the line, where the RT and RG have released to block the nickel and the Mike; Z runs his cornerback off. Right, a middle screen to the back: the tackles push the ends wide and past the quarterback, the guards and center let the tackles through and release straight upfield to the linebackers, and the back slips into the middle behind the rushers, in the space they left."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("te", "mid")):
    if kind == "te":
        p = Play(spread(y_inline=True), nickel(extra={"NB": (5.0, 8.4), "RCB": (7.0, 15.0)}), los=35, to_go=None)
        for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
        go_to(p, "RG", (2.8, 3.6), "block", via=[(-1.6, 1.8)], speed=2.4)       # set, then the Mike
        go_to(p, "RT", (2.2, 7.2), "block", via=[(-1.6, 3.4)], speed=2.4)       # set, then the nickel
        go_to(p, "Y", (-1.0, 5.2), "block", speed=0.8)                          # block the end for a count ...
        go_to(p, "Y", (-2.4, 8.4), "route", delay=0.2, speed=3.5)               # ... then slide out
        go_to(p, "Y", (9.0, 10.4), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(1.0, 9.6)])
        go_to(p, "Z", (14.0, 14.5), "route")
        go_to(p, "QB", (-8.8, -0.4), speed=2.2)
        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "Y", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "Y" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        go_to(p, "SDE", (-5.4, 2.6), "rush", speed=3.4)
        go_to(p, "SDT", (-5.0, 1.0), "rush", speed=3.4)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.8, 18.5), window=(-11.0, 15.5))
        for k, end in (("NB", (3.0, 7.8)), ("MIKE", (3.6, 3.8)), ("RCB", (11.0, 15.0))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, -6.6, 11.8, "Y: block a count,\nthen slide out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Tight end screen")
    else:
        p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
        go_to(p, "LT", (-3.2, -5.0), "block", speed=2.6)                         # push the ends wide
        go_to(p, "RT", (-3.2, 5.0), "block", speed=2.6)
        go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, -2.4), "block", via=[(-1.7, -1.6)], speed=2.4)     # set, let the tackle go, release
        go_to(p, "C", (3.6, 1.6), "block", via=[(-1.7, 0.0)], speed=2.4)
        go_to(p, "RG", (3.0, 5.0), "block", via=[(-1.7, 1.6)], speed=2.4)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -1.6), speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.6, -0.4), "route", delay=0.7, speed=2.5)
        go_to(p, "RB", (9.0, -0.3), "run", delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-9.0, 0.6), speed=2.2)
        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "RB", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        for k, end in (("WDE", (-4.4, -6.2)), ("SDE", (-4.4, 6.2)), ("WDT", (-7.2, -1.4)), ("SDT", (-7.2, 2.0))):
            go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.6)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-11.0, 15.5))
        for k, end in (("WILL", (3.8, -2.6)), ("MIKE", (4.0, 1.8))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), (q.d + 2.0, q.w)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        say(fld, p, -9.6, -8.0, "tackles push\nthe ends wide", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 8.4, 6.6, "G, C, G release\nto the LBs", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -9.4, 6.4, "DTs let\nthrough", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Middle screen")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The **tight end screen** is the slow screen run with a tight end: he blocks the end for a count, which
is exactly what defenders expect a tight end to do, then slides out behind the line on his side. It is a
good call against defenses that bring the edge rusher hard, because the rusher is the man the tight end just
let go. The **middle screen** puts the back in the middle of the field instead of the flat. The tackles
push the ends wide, as they do on any dropback; the guards and center let the defensive tackles through and
release straight upfield at the linebackers; the back slips into the space the defensive tackles just left.
It punishes interior pass rushers who get upfield fast, and linebackers who drop deep on passing downs.

::: {.callout-important title="Why screens exist"}
Every good pass rush has the same weakness: its rushers are trying to get *upfield* as fast as possible,
toward the quarterback. A screen uses that against them. It turns the rushers' speed into distance from the
ball, and it turns the five biggest people on the field, who are usually stuck at the line, into blockers in
open space. The price is that a screen gives up the rest of the passing game for one snap, needs precise
timing from seven or more players, and turns into a loss, or worse, if the defense recognizes it.
:::

## Screens punish pressure

The logic of the screen predicts something you can check: **screens should get better the more defenders
rush.** Every extra rusher is one more defender running away from the ball, and one fewer defender in front
of it.

Watch it against a six-man blitz. In @fig-screen-blitz the defense shows pressure before the snap: both
linebackers walk up into the gaps beside the center (a [double A-gap mug](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-a-gap-mug),
built in [Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd)), and behind them the
defensive backs play man coverage with no deep safety. Six rushers, five protectors plus the back.

```{python}
#| label: fig-screen-blitz
#| fig-cap: "The slow screen against a six-man blitz, frame by frame (simulated, BDB-format). (1) Six defenders rush; the Mike and Will (ringed) come through the middle. (2) The LT, LG and C let their men go and release left; the back, who appeared to pick up a blitzer, slides out behind them. (3) Four rushers converge on the quarterback, who throws over them. (4) The back catches it with three linemen in front of him and only the free safety, who was covering him from eight yards away, to beat. Every blitzer is now behind the play."
def screen_vs_blitz():
    dfn = nickel(extra={"MIKE": (1.5, 0.8), "WILL": (1.5, -0.8), "WDT": (1.0, -2.6), "LCB": (6.0, -15.5),
                        "RCB": (6.0, 15.5)},
                 shell="zero")
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
    for k in ("RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-1.4, -3.4), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LT", (2.8, -8.2), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "LG", (-1.4, -1.8), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, -5.0), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.3, 0.0), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "C", (1.2, -6.4), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0, via=[(-0.4, -4.4)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -2.0), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, -7.4), "route", delay=0.35, speed=3.4, via=[(-4.4, -4.6)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (9.0, -9.0), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-1.5, -8.0), (3.0, -8.0)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-8.6, 0.2), speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-10.4, 0.8), speed=1.6)
    p.pass_to("RB", t=2.0)
    go_to(p, "X", (15.0, -15.5), "route")
    go_to(p, "H", (5.0, -9.4), "route")
    go_to(p, "Y", (8.0, 9.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "Z", (12.0, 15.0), "route")
    # the rush: the screen side lets them through; they converge on the quarterback
    go_to(p, "WILL", (-8.0, -2.6), "rush", speed=4.4, via=[(-1.0, -1.2)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (-7.4, 2.4), "rush", speed=4.2, via=[(-1.0, 0.6)])
    go_to(p, "WDT", (-9.0, 0.4), "rush", speed=4.4, via=[(-1.0, -0.8)])
    go_to(p, "WDE", (-6.4, -4.6), "rush", speed=4.2, via=[(-1.6, -4.6)])
    go_to(p, "SDT", (-0.4, 2.0), speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "SDE", (-0.6, 4.4), speed=1.2)
    # man coverage: each defender runs with his receiver; the free safety has the back
    go_to(p, "LCB", (15.0, -15.0), speed=6.5)
    go_to(p, "SS", (6.0, -9.0), speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "NB", (9.0, 8.5), speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "RCB", (12.5, 14.5), speed=5.5)
    go_to(p, "FS", (5.0, -5.0), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "FS", (4.6, -8.0), speed=5.0)
    return p


sp = screen_vs_blitz()
play_movie(sp, [0.0, 1.2, 2.0, 2.8],
           notes=["six show blitz: the Mike and\nWill stand in the A gaps",
                  "LT, LG, C let them go and\nrelease; the back slides out",
                  "four rushers converge;\nthe throw goes over them",
                  "three linemen in front;\nevery blitzer is behind the play"],
           rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE), ("RB", style.THIRD)),
           lateral=(-20.0, 8.0), window=(-12.0, 13.0), throw_t=2.0)
```

The data agrees, strikingly. FTN's charters count the pass rushers on every dropback, so we can split
pass attempts by how many came after the quarterback.

```{python}
#| label: fig-screen-rushers
#| fig-cap: "Screens get better as the rush gets bigger. EPA per pass attempt by the number of pass rushers, 2022-2025 regular seasons: screens of every kind (blue), running back screens alone (aqua) and every other pass (orange). Against three rushers (with eight defenders in coverage), screens are among the worst plays in football; against six or more, they beat ordinary passes. The six-plus group is small (labelled counts), so read its exact height loosely and its direction firmly. Data: nflverse play-by-play with FTN charting via nflreadpy."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.7))
xs = [3, 4, 5, 6]
lab = {3: "3", 4: "4", 5: "5", 6: "6+"}
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
series = [("Other passes", SCR[~SCR["screen"]].set_index("rushers"), style.SERIES[1]),
          ("All screens", SCR[SCR["screen"]].set_index("rushers"), style.SERIES[0]),
          ("RB screens", RBS, style.SERIES[2])]
for name, df, col in series:
    df = df.reindex(xs)
    ax.plot(xs, df["epa"], color=col, marker="o", ms=6, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.2, lw=2, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(name, (6, df["epa"].iloc[-1]), xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center",
                fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
    if name != "Other passes":
        for x_, (n_, e_) in zip(xs, zip(df["n"], df["epa"])):
            off = (0, -12) if name == "All screens" else ((-20, -2) if x_ == 4 else (0, 8))
            ax.annotate(f"n={int(n_):,}", (x_, e_), xytext=off, textcoords="offset points", ha="center",
                        fontsize=6.3, color=style.MUTED)
ax.set_xticks(xs, [lab[x] for x in xs])
ax.set_xlim(2.7, 6.9)
ax.set_ylim(-0.25, 0.2)
ax.set_xlabel("Pass rushers on the play", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per pass attempt", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.set_title("The more they rush, the better the screen", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-screen-rushers from left to right. Against a three-man rush, all screens averaged
`{python} f"{SCR.set_index(['screen', 'rushers']).loc[(True, 3), 'epa']:+.2f}"` EPA per attempt: the defense
has eight players in coverage and no rushers to fool, so the screen is just a short pass into a crowd.
Against six or more rushers they averaged `{python} f"{SCR.set_index(['screen', 'rushers']).loc[(True, 6), 'epa']:+.2f}"`,
better than other passes against the same pressure. Running back screens, the purest version of the idea,
climb the most steeply.

Two cautions. First, selection: offenses call screens when they *expect* pressure, and a screen called into a
blitz is likely to be the right call at the right moment, so these averages flatter screens a little. Second,
the typical screen is not a great play: across all rush counts, screens averaged
`{python} f"{LG_SCREEN_EPA:+.2f}"` EPA per attempt, below ordinary passes. Screens are not an engine of an
offense. They are a **tax on pressure**: a play that makes blitzing expensive, so that the defense rushes four
more often, which helps every other pass the offense throws. Screens made up about
`{python} pct(SCREEN_SHARE.loc[2025])` of pass attempts in 2025, and `{python} pct(SCR_RB_SHARE)` of screens
over 2022–2025 went to running backs.

## A short history

**Play-action** is as old as the legal forward pass (1906): as soon as a team could throw, faking a run
first was the obvious way to make a defense hesitate.[^forward] What changed over the twentieth century was
how *systematically* offenses built it in. The Wing-T of the 1950s made the run fake and the bootleg (its
waggle) part of a series in which every play looked like the others, the idea you met in
[03-05](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd).

The modern NFL bootleg game runs through **Mike Shanahan** and **Gary Kubiak** in Denver. Kubiak was the
Broncos' offensive coordinator from 1995 through 2005 under Shanahan, alongside Alex Gibbs's outside zone run
game of [03-02](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd), and John Elway, in the last four seasons of his
career, made faking the stretch and rolling away from it a staple. The pairing became a coaching tree's signature. Kyle Shanahan, Mike's son, was the Atlanta Falcons'
offensive coordinator in 2016, when Matt Ryan, throwing off play-action and boots, was named the league's
MVP. Kyle took the system to San Francisco as head coach in 2017, and Sean McVay and Matt LaFleur, who had
coached on his offensive staffs in Washington (and, for LaFleur, Atlanta), carried it to the Rams and the
Packers.[^tree]

Then the data caught up with the coaches. In 2018 Sean McVay's Rams went 13–3 and reached the Super Bowl
with Jared Goff throwing off play-action more than any quarterback in the league, on roughly a third of his
dropbacks.[^rams18] In the same year Baldwin and Hermsmeyer published the analyses described above, showing
that play-action's value did not depend on the run game. Play-action rates rose across the league
afterward. In FTN's charting the league used play-action on `{python} pct(PA_RATE.loc[2022])` of dropbacks in
2022 and `{python} pct(PA_RATE.loc[2025])` in 2025, with the return of the under-center formation (see
[Classic Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd)) helping push it up.

**Screens** are just as old, and no one owns them. The screen game most associated with the modern NFL is
**Andy Reid**'s. Reid learned the West Coast offense under Mike Holmgren in Green Bay, and from his first
years as a head coach in Philadelphia (from 1999) his teams threw running back screens as a core play, not a
gimmick, with Brian Westbrook as their best-known weapon in the 2000s. He took the same habits to Kansas City
in 2013.[^reid]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018"}
**The season:** McVay's second year, 13–3, a loss to New England in Super Bowl LIII. Goff threw off
play-action more often than any other quarterback, nearly always from the same 11-personnel, tight-split
formations the Rams used for their outside zone runs with Todd Gurley (see the film room in
[Spread and Modern Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)).

**What to notice:**

- The *match*. Line steps, back's path and receivers' splits are identical on the run and the fake. Try to
  call run or pass from the first step; you will be wrong often, and so were linebackers.
- The *crossers*. A large share of the big plays are receivers running across the field at 10–15 yards,
  behind linebackers who stepped up: the window of @fig-lb-void.
- The *boots*. Goff rolling away from outside zone with the flat, crosser and over routes, often after
  pre-snap motion has moved a receiver to the boot side.
- What went wrong in the Super Bowl: the Rams scored three points. New England's defense held up against the
  run looks and gave the crossers no room, a reminder that a play-action game still needs receivers who beat
  coverage. <!-- VERIFY: before adding detail on New England's Super Bowl LIII plan (man coverage, six-man fronts), find a breakdown -->
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks 2025"}
**The season:** Klint Kubiak's one year as Seattle's offensive coordinator, with Sam Darnold at
quarterback, ending in a 29–13 win over New England in Super Bowl LX.[^lx] Kubiak is Gary Kubiak's son, and
his offense was the Denver tree in its 2025 form: outside zone from tight formations and the boots and
play-action that pair with it. In FTN's charting, Seattle's play-action dropbacks averaged
`{python} f"{team25.loc['SEA', 'epa_pa']:+.2f}"` EPA, against `{python} f"{team25.loc['SEA', 'epa_no']:+.2f}"`
on its other dropbacks, `{python} "the biggest gap in the league" if TOP_GAIN == "SEA" else "one of the biggest gaps in the league"`
(@fig-pa-teams).

**What to do:** watch any Seahawks game from 2025 and keep two counts: how many dropbacks start with a run
fake, and how many of those move the quarterback out of the pocket. Then watch the linebackers on each fake
with this chapter's checklist. Kubiak was hired as the Raiders' head coach for 2026, so this was one season's
offense, not Seattle's current one.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs 2022–2025, the screen game"}
**The record:** in FTN's charting, the Chiefs threw `{python} int(kc.loc['KC', 'n'])` screens over the four
seasons, `{python} "more than any other team" if kc.index[0] == "KC" else "among the most in the league"`,
and averaged `{python} f"{kc.loc['KC', 'epa']:+.2f}"` EPA on them, when the league average screen was worth
`{python} f"{LG_SCREEN_EPA:+.2f}"`. Most teams use screens as a tax on pressure; Reid's offense gets value
from them.

**What to notice:**

- The *sell*. Watch the Chiefs' linemen on a running back screen: they pass-set, punch and give ground as if
  in a real protection before releasing. A lazy release is the most common way screens die, and Kansas City's
  rarely look lazy.
- The *variety*. Running back slow screens, tunnel screens to receivers, tight end screens, screens off
  play-action and screens after motion: the defense cannot simply key one look.
- The *timing against pressure*. Watch what the Chiefs call on downs when an opponent has been blitzing;
  the screen is often the punishment.
:::

## The numbers: who fakes, and does it work?

Now the league-wide picture. In 2025 offenses used play-action on `{python} pct(PA_RATE.loc[2025])` of
dropbacks, and those dropbacks averaged `{python} f"{PA_EPA25:+.2f}"` EPA, against
`{python} f"{NO_EPA25:+.2f}"` for dropbacks without a fake; their success rate was
`{python} pct(PA_SR25)` against `{python} pct(NO_SR25)`. @fig-pa-teams breaks that down by team.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pa-teams
#| fig-cap: "Play-action by team, 2025 regular season. Each row is a team: EPA per dropback without a run fake (orange) and with one (blue); the line between them is the boost the fake gave that team. The right-hand column is the team's play-action rate (share of its dropbacks that began with a fake). Teams are sorted by that rate. Data: nflverse play-by-play with FTN charting via nflreadpy; dropbacks include sacks and scrambles."
t = team25.sort_values("rate")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.6))
y = np.arange(len(t))
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
ax.hlines(y, t["epa_no"], t["epa_pa"], color=style.GRID, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(t["epa_no"], y, s=30, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=3, label="No run fake", edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6)
ax.scatter(t["epa_pa"], y, s=30, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=4, label="Play-action", edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6)
ax.set_yticks(y, t.index, fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
xmax = float(max(t["epa_pa"].max(), t["epa_no"].max())) + 0.07
ax.set_xlim(float(min(t["epa_pa"].min(), t["epa_no"].min())) - 0.05, xmax + 0.12)
for yi, (rate, team) in enumerate(zip(t["rate"], t.index)):
    ax.text(xmax + 0.1, yi, f"{100 * rate:.0f}%", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
ax.text(xmax + 0.1, len(t) - 0.2, "PA rate", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom", ha="right",
        fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(t) + 0.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("Most offenses are better when they fake", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three things stand out in @fig-pa-teams.

**Most teams were better with the fake.** `{python} N_BETTER25` of 32 offenses averaged more EPA on
play-action dropbacks than on their others. That is a single season, and some teams' play-action samples
are only a hundred-odd plays, so individual gaps bounce around from year to year. The league-wide pattern
does not.

**The heaviest users build their passing game on their run game.** McVay's Rams led the league at
`{python} pct(team25.loc['LA', 'rate'])` and Ben Johnson's Bears were next at `{python} pct(team25.loc['CHI', 'rate'])`.
Several other offenses from the Shanahan family tree sat in the top half (McDaniel's Dolphins, LaFleur's
Packers, Kubiak's Seahawks), though Shanahan's own 49ers ranked only `{python} ordinal(int(RANK['SF']))` in
2025. These are offenses whose runs and passes are designed to look alike before and just after the snap.

**Some good offenses barely fake.** The lowest rates belong to teams built around a shotgun quarterback
who wins from the pocket, where a fake looks less like a run (the Chiefs were near the bottom). Low use is a
style, not a mistake: a fake is worth most when it looks like your real run, and some offenses' real runs are
not the ones defenses fear.

Why doesn't everyone fake on every snap, if it is worth that much? Partly selection again: offenses fake when
the situation makes the run believable (first-and-10, second-and-short), and the extra EPA partly belongs to
those situations. And partly because a fake only works while the defense must respect the run. On
third-and-9, nobody bites.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Play-action is a deep-ball play." Some of it is, but the biggest difference in the data is *after* the catch.
Over 2022–2025 play-action passes traveled about as far in the air as other passes but gained about
`{python} f"{YAC[True] - YAC[False]:.1f}"` more yards after the catch on average. The typical play-action
completion is a crosser or a boot route caught in space vacated by a linebacker, not a bomb.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the linebackers' feet"}
**Before the snap**

- **Under center?** About four of every five under-center dropbacks begin with a run fake. When the
  quarterback lines up under the center, think run *or* play-action, not dropback.
- **The run look.** Two tight ends, a back seven yards deep, receivers in tight splits: this is the formation
  the offense runs outside zone from, which makes it the formation it fakes from.
- **The down and distance.** First-and-10 and second-and-short are play-action downs; third-and-long is not.

**At the snap: watch the linebackers' feet, not the ball**

- Did they step *forward*? Count the steps. Two steps up on a fake is a win for the offense.
- Did the guard in front of them fire out low, or pop up? If he popped up and they stayed home, the fake did
  not work, and the throw will be harder.

**In the first two seconds**

- Did the quarterback turn his back to the defense (under-center fake) or ride the back (shotgun)?
- Did he roll away from the fake? Find the backside end: did he chase (the boot wins) or stay home (watch for
  the quick throw to the flat, or a protected boot with a pulling guard)?
- **Linemen running downfield before the throw?** It's a screen. Which ones released, and to which side? Did
  the rushers run past the back?

**After the play (on the replay)**

- How many yards did the crosser gain *after* the catch? That is the space the linebackers left.
- On a screen, count the blockers in front of the catch and the rushers behind it.

**For your prediction log** ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
on every under-center snap, write *run*, *PA* or *boot* before the snap. Then, when the defense blitzes on a
passing down, write *screen?* and see how often you are right.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the shot"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-shot
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-2 at midfield, third quarter. The offense is in 21 personnel in the I formation. The defense has walked its strong safety down to the line of scrimmage on the tight end's side and has one deep safety (ringed), about 13 yards off the ball. It has stopped the last three runs near the line, its linebackers shooting forward at the snap."
off = i_form()
dfn = [q.moved(d=1.4, w=8.0) if q.key == "SS" else (q.moved(d=4.3, w=5.2) if q.key == "SAM" else q)
       for q in even_front(cb_w=13.5, shell="one")]
dfn = [q.moved(w=-14.5) if q.key == "LCB" else (q.moved(w=14.5) if q.key == "RCB" else q) for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=2)
p.highlight("FS", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-9.0, 17.0))
say(fld, p, 10.6, 5.0, "one deep safety", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 4.4, 11.4, "SS down:\neight near\nthe box", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

**The offense has run the ball six times in its last eight plays. What should it call here, and what is the
one defender the play is aimed at?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A play-action shot, aimed at the deep safety.** Everything about the picture invites it. The defense has
committed eight players to stopping the run, so only three defenders are deep enough to matter on a deep pass:
two cornerbacks and one safety. The linebackers have been rewarded for shooting forward, so a good fake will move
them. And the free safety, the only player who protects the middle of the field deep, is the one the fake
targets: if he takes two steps forward when the back hits the line, a deep post goes over his head. Pair the
post with a deep over route from the other side (the yankee idea in @fig-shot-play) and he cannot cover both.

The down and distance make it cheap. On second-and-2, an incompletion leaves third-and-2, still a comfortable
running down. That is exactly why coaches call shots here and why the data in
[01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd), showing most offenses run on
second-and-short, matters: the defense *expects* the run, so the fake is believed.

What would make it a bad call? A defense that kept two safeties deep and played the run with seven, or a
protection problem: the shot needs three seconds, so the offense keeps eight in to block.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the end who won't bite"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-boot
#| fig-cap: "Same two-tight-end look the offense has run outside zone right from all game. On each of its last two naked bootlegs left, the backside end (ringed) did not chase the run fake: he stepped upfield and outside and waited for the quarterback (dashed orange), and both times the quarterback had to throw the ball away. It is first-and-10."
p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=30, to_go=10)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 13.5), window=(-9.5, 13.0))
branch(fld, p, [(1.0, -4.0), (-0.6, -5.6), (-4.8, -6.8)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.5)
say(fld, p, -7.6, -10.6, "what the end did\non the last two boots", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

**What has the end taken away, what has he given up, and what are two good calls from this look?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**He has taken away the naked boot and given up the outside zone cutback.** An end who stays home and waits
for the quarterback is the one defender the naked bootleg cannot survive (@fig-naked-boot, right). But an end
who stays home on the boot is not chasing the outside zone run from behind either, so on the real run the
backside of the play is softer: the cutback lane he used to close is open.

**Two good calls:**

1. **Outside zone right**, and let the back cut back. The end's new habit has taken him out of the run
   play's backside pursuit.
2. **A protected bootleg** (@fig-boot-family, left): the same fake and the same boot, but a guard pulls to kick
   the end out. The end is now a blocked defender, and the quarterback gets the edge he wanted. The risk is the
   tell of a pulling guard, which is why it is a call to make after the defense has adjusted, not before.

A third option is a **keeper the other way** (a run fake and the quarterback keeping it to the *play* side)
if that end's teammates have also started leaving the run side early. This is how the play-action game talks to
itself across a game: every adjustment the defense makes to stop one play loosens its grip on another.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: name it after the snap"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-screen
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-7, shotgun, 11 personnel. The picture is frozen 1.9 seconds after the snap; the faint lines show where every player has come from (offense blue, defense orange). Look at the offensive linemen on the left, the running back, and the quarterback's depth."
p = slow_screen(Play(spread(), nickel(), los=40, to_go=7))
for k, end in (("WDE", (-7.4, -2.6)), ("WDT", (-7.0, -0.2)), ("SDT", (-1.0, 2.0)), ("SDE", (-1.2, 4.4))):
    go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.6)
for k, end in (("WILL", (3.1, -8.2)), ("MIKE", (3.4, -4.8)), ("SS", (5.4, -11.6)), ("LCB", (13.0, -16.0))):
    go_to(p, k, end, speed=2.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))
fld = moment(ax, p, 1.9, lateral=(-19.5, 12.5), window=(-11.5, 17.5), mark_r=0.8)
q = p.position("QB", 1.9)
say(fld, p, q[0] + 0.6, q[1] + 5.2, "Q at about\n9 yards", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

**What play is this, which side is it going to, and why is it legal for the left tackle, left guard and center
to be past the line of scrimmage?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A slow screen to the running back, to the left.** Three signs, in the order you should look for them:

1. **Linemen downfield before the throw.** The LT, LG and C have released past the line toward the left. On a
   normal pass that is a foul; here they are getting in front of the receiver. Their side is the screen side.
2. **Rushers let through.** The left end and tackle have been allowed to run free at the quarterback, who has
   drifted back to about nine yards to pull them deeper, so they will be far from the ball.
3. **The back slipping out.** He stepped up as if to block, and is now sliding out to the left behind the
   rushers, where the ball will come.

**Why it is legal:** the one-yard limit on linemen downfield applies only to passes thrown *beyond* the line of
scrimmage. This pass will be caught behind it, so the linemen can be as far downfield as they like when the ball
is thrown.

It is not a swing route: on a swing, the line keeps pass-blocking and the ball comes out in about a second. Here
the line has released and the quarterback is still holding the ball at nearly two seconds, waiting for the rush to
arrive and go by.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Play-action works on the linebackers' run-fit triggers.** Defenders near the line must react to run
  signals fast; a fake that shows those signals (low line steps, the back's path, the handoff) moves them
  forward and opens the space behind them. It buys space, not protection.
- **It does not need a good run game.** Baldwin's 2018 analysis and this chapter's 2022–2025 rerun agree: a
  team's rushing efficiency barely predicts its play-action boost. What matters is that the fake **looks exactly
  like the real run**. Under-center play-action, the most convincing fake, was the most productive dropback in
  football over 2022–2025.
- The fake sends the ball to **three windows**: behind the linebackers (crossers, most of the value, much of it
  after the catch), behind the safeties (the **shot play**, with extra blockers and two or three receivers), and
  to the side the defense left (the **bootleg**).
- The **bootleg** moves the launch point away from the defense's flow, with three receivers at three depths. The
  **naked** boot bets that the end chases; the **keeper**, the **protected boot** and the **leak** answer the
  defense's adjustments to it.
- A **screen** invites the rush, releases linemen in front of a receiver behind the line (legal, because the pass
  does not cross the line) and throws over the rushers. **Slow, tunnel, jailbreak, tight end and middle** screens
  vary who catches it and where the blockers go. A **swing** or **flare** is a route, not a screen: nobody
  releases to block.
- **Screens punish pressure.** Their value climbs with every extra rusher; against a soft rush they are among the
  worst plays in football. They are a tax that keeps defenses from blitzing freely.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From diagrams to real tracking data.** The animations in this chapter are gridiron simulations in NFL Big Data
Bowl (BDB) coordinates, the format of the league's public tracking-data competition. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release
(2022 season, weeks 1–9) records every player ten times a second, and its `plays.csv` marks each play's
`playAction` and `dropbackType`, so you can find real bootlegs and watch the linebackers step up on the fake. The
data needs a free Kaggle login, so this code is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
# play-action passes on which the quarterback rolled out by design (a bootleg or a rollout)
boots = plays[(plays["playAction"] == True)
              & plays["dropbackType"].astype(str).str.contains("ROLLOUT", case=False)]
print(len(boots), "play-action rollouts")
g, pl = boots.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.7, 1.5, 2.3])   # snap, the fake, the boot, the throw
```
